sections.title: The Shepherds of Israel
observations: Ezekiel begins this chapter by addressing the leaders of Israel, whom he refers to as shepherds. The metaphor of shepherding is significant in the biblical context, representing care, guidance, and responsibility for the people.

God condemns these shepherds for their failure to care for the flock. Instead of nurturing and protecting the people, they have exploited and neglected them, leading to their scattering and suffering.
This section serves as a critique of spiritual leaders who prioritize their own interests over the well-being of those they are meant to guide.

sections.title: God as the True Shepherd
observations: In response to the failures of the human shepherds, God declares that He Himself will take on the role of the shepherd for His people. This is a profound declaration of God's commitment to His flock.
God promises to seek out the lost, bring back the strayed, bind up the injured, and strengthen the weak. This highlights God's compassion and active involvement in the lives of His people.
The imagery of God as a shepherd is a comforting and powerful reminder of His care and sovereignty.

sections.title: Judgment and Restoration
observations: God announces that He will judge between the sheep, indicating that there will be accountability for the actions of both the leaders and the people.
He promises to establish a covenant of peace and to provide for His people, leading them to a place of safety and security. This points to a future hope and restoration for Israel.
The chapter concludes with a promise of a Davidic shepherd, which is often interpreted as a messianic prophecy pointing to Jesus Christ.

importantVerses.commentary: For thus says the Lord God: 'Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out.'
I will seek the lost, and I will bring back the strayed, and I will bind up the injured, and I will strengthen the weak.

questions: What does the metaphor of shepherding reveal about God's character and His relationship with His people?
How can we apply the lessons from the failures of the shepherds in our own spiritual leadership today?
In what ways does the promise of a Davidic shepherd point to the person and work of Jesus Christ?
